newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African 1996 inflation lowest in 24 years.
newsitem.headline: S.African 1996 inflation lowest in 24 years.

text.p: South African consumer price inflation dropped to 7.4 percent in 1996, its lowest average rate in 24 years, despite a rise in December.
The inflation rate rose to 9.4 percent last month -- its higest monthly level since June 1995 -- but economists said on Tuesday that price rises still appeared to be under control.
The rise in the consumer price index from November's 9.2 percent brought the average rate for the year to 7.4 percent compared with 8.7 percent in 1995 -- the lowest since 1972.
"The average inflation rate for last year was very good and I think in 1997 we can continue to look forward to single digit inflation," said Carole Mason, group economist at Investec.
"We're working on an average inflation rate for this year of 8.5 percent."
Other analysts said the inflation rate was likely to creep up in the early months of 1997, perhaps nosing above 10 percent in April or May, before moving down again in the second half of the year.

The full effects of the rand's fall of a fifth against a basket of currencies in 1996 had yet to feed through the system fully, and would continue to show up in higher imported product costs for a few months yet.
But the currency's strong rebound this month augured well for a better inflation picture later in the year.
Analysts noted that one-off increase in housing and fuel costs were the main drivers behind a relatively high 1.0 percent month-on-month increase in South African inflation in December.
Housing costs jumped due to an increase of one percentage point in interest rates on mortgage bonds while a hike in gasoline prices pushed up the transport component of the index.
The December inflation data was slightly better than expected. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast a year-on-year rate of 9.6 percent.
